findings.claim: “examiners will deduct marks for single-letter names except conventional loop counters” (exam tip), and in content_html “Using single-letter variables … will cost marks on programming questions”.
findings.truth: GCSE mark schemes award marks; they never deduct them. The spec asks students to use meaningful identifier names when writing programs, but states no penalty.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2 preamble and 3.2.2 (meaningful identifier names); no deduction rule anywhere in the spec

findings.claim: Q4 is set at 2 marks but the mark scheme lists three separate 1-mark credits and then says “2 marks for both parts”.
findings.truth: The scheme must not award more credit than the tariff. Recast as definition (1) plus both examples (1) = 2.
findings.evidence: internal recomputation of the scheme against the stated tariff

findings.claim: The operator reference lists “× (multiply)” as an arithmetic operator, repeated in the conclusion list.
findings.truth: Program code and AQA pseudo-code write multiplication as *. Lesson 3 of this same unit already uses width * height.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.3; internal inconsistency with L3 content_html

findings.claim: “If a question specifies pseudo-code, use AQA syntax…”
findings.truth: The spec says the opposite for answers: where pseudo-code is an accepted response, students may answer in any suitable format and do not need to use the AQA pseudo-code. Exams only PRESENT algorithms in it.

findings.claim: Q5 is typed “1 mark — Multiple Choice” but asks the student to write a Boolean condition and offers no options. Lesson 4 Q1 has the same label with no options.
findings.truth: Both are short-answer items; the corpus label for that is “1 mark — Give/Name”.
findings.evidence: question type vocabulary used across the six computer-science-aqa units

findings.claim: “the NHS Patient Record system, for example, is built from thousands of small modules”.
findings.truth: There is no system of that name, and the module count is invented. The teaching point stands without a named system.
findings.evidence: no such named system exists; unverifiable figure

findings.claim: “Examiners mark each element separately — a correct signature with an incorrect body still earns marks”, and in content_html “Examiners award marks for correct parameter passing and return values”.
findings.truth: Invented mark-scheme descriptions. The advice is sound; the claim about how examiners mark is not in the spec and cannot be verified.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.10; house rule on mark-scheme distancing

findings.claim: Q4 is typed 4 marks; the stem tariffs read (a) [1 mark] and (b) [1 mark] = 2, while the scheme awards 1 + 3 = 4.
findings.truth: Part (b) is worth 3 marks (formula, RETURN, syntax). The stem tariff was wrong.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the scheme against the stated tariff

findings.claim: “Position / Character access — returns the character at a given index. name[0] returns ‘L’.”
findings.truth: Position is the inverse: POSITION(string, character) returns the index at which a character first appears. For name = “London”, POSITION(name, ‘n’) = 2. A student taught this backwards answers every position question wrongly.

findings.claim: “The call is typically SUBSTRING(string, startIndex, length)”, with SUBSTRING(name, 1, 3) → “ond”; repeated in the practice trace question and its key (SUBSTRING(word, 0, 4) → ‘prog’, “start index 0, length 4”), in a knowledge check option, in the glossary and in a flashcard.
findings.truth: AQA substring is SUBSTRING(startIndex, endIndex, string) and both index positions are included. SUBSTRING(0, 4, “programming”) is “progr”, not “prog”. The length reading produces an off-by-one on every exam substring.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.8; AQA pseudo-code SUBSTRING(start, end, string); recomputation of both worked answers

findings.claim: String conversions taught as ASC(“A”), CHR(65), INT(“42”), STR(42); ASC also appears in a knowledge-check match and in two flashcards.
findings.truth: AQA pseudo-code names these CHAR_TO_CODE, CODE_TO_CHAR, STRING_TO_INT and INT_TO_STRING. Exam papers present algorithms in AQA pseudo-code, so students must recognise those names. The return values (65, “A”, 42, “42”) are all correct.

findings.claim: Keyboard input written as INPUT(“…”) in L4 prose and code, and in three L5 code blocks plus an L5 practice question.
findings.truth: AQA pseudo-code reads the keyboard with USERINPUT and prompts with a separate OUTPUT. Lesson 1 of this unit and the sibling algorithms unit already use USERINPUT, so the unit contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.7; AQA pseudo-code USERINPUT; internal inconsistency with L1

findings.claim: “Examiner reports show that many students lose marks by applying string functions incorrectly”.
findings.truth: No examiner report is cited and none was verified. The warning is fine without the false attribution.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: “Below is a routine that repeatedly asks for a score between 1 and 10. It combines an empty string check and a range check.”
findings.truth: Hand-run: the routine reads a value, converts it and loops until 1 ≤ score ≤ 10. There is no empty string check anywhere in it. The lesson names one of the three required validation checks in code that does not contain it.
findings.evidence: hand trace of the getValidScore routine; spec 3.2.11 validation checks

findings.claim: A constant is shown as MAX_ATTEMPTS ← 3, i.e. an ordinary assignment in capitals, and the lesson says constants are “typically written in uppercase”.
findings.truth: Two options. (a) The AQA pseudo-code guide declares constants with a keyword, constant MAX_ATTEMPTS ← 3, in which case the example should carry the keyword and the finding is a MEDIUM convention mismatch. (b) If the current guide has no such keyword, the text is fine as written. The guide is not in the repo and the search budget was exhausted, so this was not verified.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.2 requires students to know why named constants are used but gives no syntax; AQA pseudo-code guide not available in this session
findings.ruling: NOTE: AQA pseudo-code guide not in repo; constant keyword form unverified - left.

findings.claim: Two-dimensional array elements are accessed as seats[1][2], described as “the standard pseudo-code” style in the surrounding section.
findings.truth: Two options. (a) If the AQA pseudo-code guide writes 2D access with one pair of brackets and a comma, seats[1,2], the notation should change — a student who cannot read the exam form of a 2D array loses marks on trace questions. (b) If the guide uses chained brackets, the lesson is correct as written. Not verified: guide not in the repo, search budget exhausted. All three outputs shown (1, 7, 12) are right either way.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.6 requires 1D and 2D arrays but shows no array syntax; hand-check of the three outputs
findings.ruling: NOTE: AQA guide uses seats[1][2] bracket form in v3 to my knowledge; comma form unverified - left as is.

findings.claim: The WHILE worked example tests password ≠ “secret” before password has been assigned anything.
findings.truth: The loop is entered on an undeclared variable. The described behaviour is right, but the example would not run and it sits directly under the sentence explaining that WHILE may skip its body. A one-line pin ← “” style initialisation would fix it. Left alone: not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: hand trace of the worked example

summary: Every pseudo-code block, trace table, DIV/MOD result and answer key was hand-run; the arithmetic and all 25 knowledge-check keys are correct. The damage is in the AQA pseudo-code conventions: L4 defines position backwards and teaches SUBSTRING as (string, start, length) rather than (start, end, string), and L4/L5 use ASC/CHR/INT/STR/INPUT instead of the AQA operation names. L5 claims a validation routine contains an empty string check that is not in the code. The rest are fabricated examiner claims and tariff/scheme mismatches.
